title: Donnchadh mac Iain is born at Cnoc bhàn
summary: A cutter's widow of Cnoc bhàn brings her second son to the stag's teachers rather than send him to the vein at ten years old, judging one son owed to the coal enough for her house. He grows up among the school's chests of strike-books before he grows up among the seams.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain is set to the old leaves
summary: In a thin winter Cnoc bhàn's masters set the young teacher Donnchadh mac Iain to clearing dead apprentices' leaves from the school's chests, a task given him more as punishment than trust. He begins, instead, a private tally of when in a cutter's years the coal comes brightest.

title: Aonghas Cam answers the tally
summary: The eldest teacher of Cnoc bhàn, Aonghas Cam, hears Donnchadh mac Iain's tally at the midwinter gathering and answers, as the house had always answered, that the vein knows a cutter's blood and the years only show what was already there. The two teachings begin to divide the room.

title: The house at Cnoc bhàn sits in two halves
summary: By the eighth year of Donnchadh mac Iain's yearly tally, those who hear him to the end of it and those who answer him before he finishes have come, without any master's ordering, to sit on opposite sides of the long room at every midwinter gathering.

title: The twenty-two leave Cnoc bhàn
summary: Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two hearers load copies of the strike-books they judge their own onto two borrowed carts and walk south to Muileann chaol. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft; Donnchadh calls it copying, since every leaf they made a copy of stands where it always stood.

title: Muileann chaol's reeve houses the school
summary: The reeve of Muileann chaol lets Donnchadh mac Iain's twenty-two hearers a millwright's storehouse for a rent none of them can pay in coin, taken instead that first winter in mended roofs and re-hung doors for half the town.

title: Muileann chaol's books are ruled to keep no parentage
summary: Donnchadh mac Iain sets the rule for the new school's strike-books: no cutter's father, mother or house is written on a leaf, only the name, the day and the stroke. More than one of the twenty-two finds the old habit slower to unlearn than the rule was to set down.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain writes north
summary: Seventy years old and less able to travel, Donnchadh mac Iain sends the first letter to Cnoc bhàn, addressed to the house rather than to any one master, asking whether its own century-and-a-half of leaves shows the same rise with a cutter's years that his own count once showed.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain dies at Muileann chaol
summary: Donnchadh mac Iain dies at eighty in the storehouse-schoolhouse his twenty-two hearers first took shelter in forty years before, having taught six generations whose leaves carry no father's or mother's name. He is buried under a leaf of oiled hide cut with one word: one who writes.

title: Raonaid Dhubh is born at Dùn ìseal
summary: A clerk's daughter is born at Dùn ìseal in the same year Donnchadh mac Iain dies, given the name Raonaid Dhubh for the black hair she keeps unusually from her first day.

title: Raonaid Dhubh takes Coimheadaiche na Lasrach's stool
summary: Raonaid Dhubh comes to Coimheadaiche na Lasrach's own chest of clerks at twenty, an elder cousin's death leaving the stool empty at a season when no one else in the room wants the sitting of it, and reads there, among other papers, the growing archive of letters between Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chaol.

title: Both schools ask the new Keeper for a ruling
summary: Within her first year holding the cup, Raonaid Dhubh receives word from both Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chaol asking her to say, once and plainly, which school's reading of the vein is the truer, as every Keeper before her has been asked and never once has answered.

title: The scholars of Muileann chaol cannot read Cnoc ghorm's stone
summary: Scholars of the second school travel east to Cnoc ghorm to read the standing stone at the town's centre, and spend the better part of a day turning its worn face to the light without making out a single letter of its cutting.

title: Baile ghorm's diggers find only ash
summary: A company from Baile ghorm breaks into the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin by night on the strength of an old tale of riches, and finds at dawn nothing beneath the stone but cold, undisturbed ash that no fire any of them can name had left.

title: The diggers' road earns its name
summary: The road the families of Baile ghorm keep in repair as their penance, from their own town south to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, is by this year known in the southern hills by no other name than the diggers' road, kept long past any term Coimheadaiche na Lasrach's sentence set.
